coredata.dc:description: The identification and monitoring of changes in land use patterns for pond construction compared to the existing river area and fish production from ponds and rivers by spatiotemporal analysis of Bangladesh, at large, is unknown. This study aims to identify aquaculture clusters developed over the last two decades (2001-2020) in a spatiotemporal approach by applying geographic information systems (GIS) and forecast pond area, pond, and river production for the next 10 years using the autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) model based on secondary data collected from the Department of Fisheries (DoF). The results show that a high volume of pond area and production is concentrated in north-west, North-central, south-west, and south-east regions of Bangladesh. River production is concentrated in south-central and south-east regions of Bangladesh, especially in Bola, Barishal, Patuakhali, Borguna, Chandpur, and Lakshmipur districts. Over the last 19 years, pond area has increased by 52.35%, aquaculture (pond) production has increased by 199%, and capture fisheries (river) has increased by 131%. Although river production has grown, it is still six times less than pond production. In south-central Bangladesh, river fish production showed a reciprocal relationship with aquaculture production. The ARIMA model forecasts that land acquisition through pond construction will increase to 3.13% of Bangladesh's total area by 2030, up from 1.71% in 2001. The pond area will be increased by approximately 75% between 2001 and 2030. In 2030, the production of aquaculture and capture fisheries will be 2.88 million MT and 0.6 million MT, respectively. Our study recommends some important strategies for policymakers to formulate a region-based approach and promote commercial upgrading of aquaculture production with modern technologies, followed by limiting land acquisition.

ce:section.ce:para: Asia accounts for nearly two-thirds of global inland capture fisheries production, with Africa as the second-largest contributor [1]. Southeast Asia is increasing their focus to inland capture and cultured fish production. Bangladesh, a Southeast Asian country, demonstrates a lower level of marine capture production compared to its inland counterpart. Therefore, there is a pressing need for Bangladesh to intensify its emphasis on aquaculture and riverine fish production to sustain the growth in fish production, an essential step for maintaining the availability of affordable protein and strengthening foreign exchange earnings.

In Bangladesh, three fish-producing sectors comprise the entire fisheries sector: inland (open water) capture fisheries, inland (closed inland and coastal water) aquaculture (culture fisheries), and marine fisheries. Pond-based fish production relies almost entirely on hatchery-based seed production, resulting in non-mutual dependence between river and pond fish production in Bangladesh [2]. Of these, pond aquaculture contributes more than 57.38% of the overall production, whereas river-based inland capture fisheries contribute only 27.72% [2].

Aquaculture encompasses various systems, such as pond culture, paddy fields, borrow pits, baors, coastal aquaculture, pens, and cage culture, all of which play a role in overall aquaculture production. Notably, pond culture stands out as the leading contributor, accounting for nearly 80% of the total aquaculture production. Land acquisition by pond construction was 1.71% of the total area of Bangladesh in 2001, which had risen to 2.72% in 2019 [2,3]. There are various historical reasons why Bangladesh has a huge number of ponds with a vast occupied area. Prior to commercialization of pond aquaculture, ponds were traditionally used as a common property resource with multiple users in the rural communities, and regularly used for bathing, washing, watering livestock, and small-scale irrigation for dykes or homestead vegetable production [4]. With the rise of commercial aquaculture, the role of ponds began to shift significantly to pond-based, semi-intensive fish farming. Generally, homestead pond owners consume a large share of their harvest, showing that pond aquaculture remains driven not only by income but also by the need for household nutrition and food availability [4].

According to the statistics of Department of Fisheries (DoF), the production of fish from rivers was 0.1 million Metric Ton (MT) in 2001-2002, while the production of fish from ponds was 0.6 million MT [3]. Over the last 19 years, corresponding fish production from rivers and ponds increased to 0.3 and 2 million MT, respectively [2], while fish production from rivers and ponds increased by slightly over two and three times, respectively. About four decades ago, when the main purpose of the homestead ponds was not a major source of fish consumption, people used to harvest the bulk of fish from the rivers. The dependency of food fish production on the rivers was because Bangladesh is one of the largest and most active deltas fed by three mighty rivers, which are connected to the Bay of Bengal. Over the years, the modest growth in fish production from the rivers was attributed to reduction of river areas and deterioration of river environment. The total area of the river was 1 million hectare (ha) in 2001-02, but it shrank to 0.8 million ha in 2007-08, a 17.23 % decrease in river area within six years [5]. The reported reasons for the shrinking of river areas are construction of upstream dams across the rivers, unplanned growth of industrial infrastructure in the river catchment area, and illegal occupation of rivers by various individuals and organizations [5,6].

This context indicates that while the rivers were once one of the main sources of fish, the reduction in river areas and fish production has greatly increased the trend of pond-based fish farming in Bangladesh. As the fish production from the rivers decreased, people initially started digging ponds and farming fish by 1996-97 (Fig. 5a).

Over time, pond farming in Bangladesh has shifted from a subsistence activity to a commercial enterprise, raising questions about its broader implications. This study aims to explore these issues by investigating the following research questions.
•
How has pond-based aquaculture expanded spatially across Bangladesh over the past two decades, and is this expansion associated with a decline in riverine fish production?
•
What are the projected trends in pond area expansion and fish production (aquaculture and riverine) in Bangladesh through 2030?
•
What policy measures can support sustainable pond-based aquaculture amid declining river fish resources?

These questions are addressed by performing a spatiotemporal analysis of the previous 19 years' district-wise 1
1 In Bangladesh, a district is an administrative unit comparable to a county or prefecture in other countries, serving as a subnational division below the regional (divisional) level. changes on river area, river production, pond area, and pond production using GIS techniques. Previous studies on aquaculture land use in Bangladesh have focused primarily on the southwestern, mangrove, and coastal regions [7–9]. A few studies were conducted on tilapia and pangasius aquaculture agglomeration externalities in Bangladesh [ 10]. To the authors’ knowledge from the existing literature, this is the first study that employs both GIS mapping to understand the previous twenty years aquaculture, riverine fish production cluster, land use scenario and deploy a time series autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) model to reveal the future ten years scenario of fish production and land use. ARIMA models, well known for their simplicity and reliance on historical observations for forecasting, demonstrate effectiveness, especially when applied to univariate datasets. Given the absence of external factors in the linear data of the current study, ARIMA is preferred over more complex models such as neural networks or random forests. Moreover, the successful application of ARIMA and other time-series models in prior research on fish production highlights its suitability [10–13].

The novelty of our study is building a link between the past and the future through spatial analysis using GIS and temporal analysis using predictive time-series modeling. There have been limited studies on predictive modeling in Bangladesh's fisheries and aquaculture sectors. Previous studies mainly focused on total fish production, while this study analyzed the total production using different approaches, such as pond and river production, including pond area and productivity.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Entire Bangladesh as the study area
ce:section.ce:para:
Bangladesh, a potential country for agricultural production, has a tropical monsoon climate characterized by wide seasonal variations in the Indian subcontinent, located explicitly beside the Bay of Bengal at a latitude of 23.6850° N and a longitude of 90.3563° E. A 710 km-long coastline is split by numerous rivers which serve as the nearly sole drainage outlet for a massive and intricate river basin that is made up of a total of 405 rivers [14]. Among them the Ganges Brahmaputra, Meghna, and their network of tributaries play a significant role in capture fisheries production. Considering this context, depending on the fish production, the entire Bangladesh was classified into seven hydrological regions include north-west, north-central, north-east, south-west, south-central, south-east, and eastern hill regions, which underwent various changes in riverine and pond fish production (Fig. S1) [15]. Bangladesh's hydrological zones exhibit distinct characteristics. In the south-west, the Khulna-Satkhira-Jessore coastal area faces challenges from cyclones, pollution, drought, and tidal and flash floods, comprising approximately 80% of prawn and shrimp aquaculture operations [8,9,16]. Flood-proofing and haor 2
2 A haor is a type of wetland ecosystem found primarily in the northeastern region of Bangladesh. Haors are bowl-shaped, floodplain depressions that are seasonally inundated, forming large, shallow lakes during the monsoon season. basin management are the top concerns in the north-east region [17]. The north-central region faces issues of significant river pollution, river encroachment, and Dhaka's water supply. The north-west, along the Brahmaputra River's right bank, tackles challenges related to drought, floods, and riverbank erosion [17]. The south-central region grapples with siltation, emphasizing enhanced cyclone protection and coastal embankment maintenance. In the south-east, farming of prawn and shrimp, a major source of naturally occurring riverine fish production, is a focal point [18]. The Chattogram Hill Tracts (CHT), situated in the Eastern Hill Region, constitute the only significant mountainous area in Bangladesh. Bandarban, Rangamati, and Khagrachhari, the three hilly districts comprising the CHT, are in the early stages of developing the aquaculture industry due to challenges such as limited water accessibility and availability of fish seed and feed [19].

This study conducted a comprehensive spatiotemporal analysis based on nationally published secondary data obtained from the Fisheries Resources Survey System (FRSS), compiled by the Department of Fisheries (DoF), Government of Bangladesh (https://fisheries.gov.bd/site/page/54ea4502-a4cb-4e33-9f29-4be8f09cf8a6/মৎস্য-পরিসংখ্যান). Pond area data were analyzed over a 19-year period (2001–02 to 2019–20), which is the earliest timeframe with consistent and spatially disaggregated records available in the national dataset. In contrast, data on pond-based aquaculture and riverine fish production spanned a longer period, from 1983 to 84 to 2019–20, covering the full extent of available production records reported by the DoF. The data extracted from the FRSS statistical yearbook were organized and inputted into an Excel spreadsheet for further analysis. To fit the ARIMA model, the datasets were transformed as needed, applying either a Box-Cox or logarithmic transformation. Furthermore, 85% of the data was allocated for training, while the remaining 15% was reserved for testing. From 2001 to 2020, data at five-year intervals (2001, 2005, 2010, 2015, and 2020) were collected to enable the visualization of significant spatial changes. Following this, the dataset underwent conversion into a comma-separated values (CSV) file and was exported back into the ArcGIS software.

A georeferenced shape file of Bangladesh was used and obtained from the website www.diva-gis.org for spatiotemporal analysis using ArcGIS (version 10.8). The ArcGIS software was utilized to import Keyhole Markup Language (KML) and shape files (SHP files) as a vector layer for GIS data processing. The Geographic Coordinate System GCS_WGS_1984 was employed in this study. Graduated colors from the Symbology tab were used to highlight the district area with its respective values, such as production, area, productivity, etc. The default classification for the field values used five classes and natural breaks. Customized classifications, such as seven classes and eight classes breaks, were used in the pond area, production, and productivity analysis by using a manual method. A single-color ramp was used for graduated color analysis. A point density plot for river production was formed using spatial analyst tools from the Arc Toolbox. Finally, after changing all graduated colors, symbols, and dot density analysis, the desired layers shown in a particular map were activated.

Data on pond area from 2001 to 02 to 2019-20 and pond and river production from 1983 to 84 to 2019-20 were compiled from twenty volumes of statistical yearbooks published by the DoF. The different time frames reflect data availability: pond area data are available for 19 years since spatial records began at the national level, while aquaculture and capture fisheries production data cover 37 years, enabling long-term trend analysis and projections. As the DoF is the sole official source, the study relied solely on its published records to ensure consistency and accuracy. Using the dataset of DoF, time series analysis was conducted using the ARIMA model introduced by Box and Jenkins [20]. ARIMA has been applied across a variety of fields, including business, weather forecasting, and fisheries production [10–12,21]. In the ARIMA (p, d, q) model, p, q, and d denote the autoregressive lags, moving average, and difference order of the process, respectively. The ARIMA (p, d, q) model equation is as follows:
Yt = φ1Yt− 1+φ2Yt− 2+ … +φpYt− p+α1 – θ1αt− 1 – α2 – θ2αt− 2 − … − αq – θqαt− q,
where φp, αq, θq, and Yt denote the AR operator, error term coefficient, parameter values of the MA operator, and dth difference, respectively [22]. In this study, a number of steps were followed to conduct time series analysis applying ARIMA. Statistical software RStudio (version-2021.09.2) was used for R programming.

Firstly, the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test was performed to estimate the test statistics, p-value, and lags to identify stationarity. The three datasets used in this study were not stationary, as seen in the graph (Fig. S2 and S3), where the mean and variance were not constant. In addition, the p-value was more than 0.05 in the ADF test, which was not significant (Table S1). The p-value was less than 0.05 in the ADF test means that time series datasets became stationary. The non-stationary data can be transformed into stationary data by taking a single or repeated difference [23].

Secondly, the estimation of q and p was done using autocorrelation function (ACF) and partial ACF (PACF), respectively. To estimate the parameters p and q for an ARIMA model, we examined PACF and ACF plots. For p (the AR order), we identified the lag where the PACF sharply cuts off and becomes insignificant, with the number of significant lags before this cut-off indicating p. For q (the MA order), we determined the lag where the ACF dropped off abruptly and remained close to zero, with the number of significant lags before this cut-off indicating q (Fig. S2 and S3). Thirdly, this stage involves determining the parameters for the selected preliminary models. The values of the model selection criteria, such as mean squared error (MSE), root mean squared error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), Akaike's information criterion (AIC), and mean error (ME), were performed to identify the best model (S1 File). The model with the best forecasting ability has the smallest error criterion value [24]. Finally, from the best model, the accuracy was checked by plotting the ACF and PACF of the residuals. Then, we modified the model when the plotted PACF and ACF did not appear as white noise. A diagnostic test of the forecast was performed using the Ljung-Box test statistic. After model selection, MSE, RMSE, MAE, MAPE, and AIC were the statistical measures used to evaluate the performance of the forecasting model. The goodness-of-fit approach for a time series is based on residuals. The models used for forecasting have residuals that meet key criteria: a mean of zero, consistent variance, no correlation, and a normal distribution [25]. One of the models exhibited a slight negative skewness (Fig. 6). Despite this, an evaluation of model's performance with diagnostic checks using L-jung test, Quantile–Quantile plot (QQ plot), and ACF plot, indicated that the residuals did not deviate significantly from normality in a way that would reduce the model's accuracy (Fig. 1 ).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Trend of pond area for aquaculture
ce:section.ce:para: Pond aquaculture expanded unevenly across regions. In the north-west districts (Bogra, Noagaon, Rajshahi, Pabna), pond areas steadily expanded, while the growth in Natore and Rangpur was relatively slower. The north-central region emerged as a major hub of pond development, with Mymensingh experiencing rapid expansion from 2001 to 2011, followed by slower growth through 2015 (Fig. 2a, c, 2d). In contrast, Dhaka saw a pronounced decline in pond area between 2001 and 2020 (Fig. 2a and e). The north-east region showed comparatively slow growth; Sylhet recorded modest increases over the two decades, while Sunamganj's pond area halved around 2015 compared to 2001 (Fig. 2a and d).

In the south-west, Jashore experienced rapid pond expansion, more than doubling its pond area over roughly a decade, while other districts like Satkhira also showed strong growth. In contrast, Khulna did not see significant pond development, as its lands were more suitable for shrimp farming. In the south-central region, river-fish producing districts such as Patuakhali, Bhola, and Barisal saw considerable pond expansion over the past two decades. The south-east, particularly Cumilla, Noakhali, Chandpur, and Lakshmipur, also exhibited high pond construction trends. Even the eastern hill districts, which initially had few or no ponds, including Khagrachari, Bandarban, and Rangamati, experienced new pond development by 2010–11. Chattogram stood out among the eastern hill districts with substantial pond growth over the 19-year period (Fig. 2a–e).

In the north-west, Dinajpur led fish production in 2001–2002, followed by Rajshahi, Naogaon, Natore, and Pabna, while by 2019–2020, Rajshahi emerged as the top-producing district, with Natore showing the highest productivity per hectare (Fig. 3 a and e). In the north-central region, Mymensingh consistently remained the largest pond production hub, with both total production and productivity increasing substantially over the two decades (Fig. 3a and e). The north-east region showed more moderate growth, with Sunamganj, Sylhet, and Maulavibazar increasing their production steadily between 2001–2002 and 2019–2020 (Fig. 3a and e). Overall, these trends highlight strong regional differences, with the north-central region driving major gains in total production, while per-hectare productivity improved across several north-west and north-east districts.

Following Mymensingh, Jashore emerged as the second-largest contributor to pond fish production in Bangladesh. Over the past two decades, Jashore experienced a dramatic expansion, with both total production and per-hectare productivity rising six-fold (Fig. 3a and e). In the south-central region, Barishal became the leading producer by 2019–2020, followed by Bhola, Patuakhali, Pirojpur, Barguna, and Jhalokati, while Bhola exhibited the most pronounced gains in productivity over time (Fig. 3).

In the south-east, Cumilla dominated pond fish production, with Noakhali, Chandpur, Brahmanbaria, Lakshmipur, and Feni forming a strong secondary tier. Cumilla also achieved the highest productivity, and most districts in this region showed consistent improvements in output per unit area (Fig. 3e). In contrast, the eastern hill region displayed highly variable trends. Chattogram's production fluctuated over time, with alternating periods of growth and decline, while Bandarban, Rangamati, and Khagrachari had no pond aquaculture in the early 2000s but began contributing after 2010. Although these hill districts entered pond-based production during the later years, their productivity remained comparatively low (Fig. 3).

The density of red dots in a district shows the quantity of fish produced by the rivers in those areas, and it has revealed the mapping of river production clusters in Bangladesh. The higher the dot concentration, the greater the production. Geospatial visualizations revealed that substantial concentrations of river production were observed in the south-central and south-east parts of Bangladesh. River fish production displayed strong regional contrasts across Bangladesh (Fig. 4 ). In the south-central region, Bhola consistently emerged as the dominant producer, followed by Barishal and Patuakhali, reflecting the importance of large river systems and floodplain connectivity in this zone. In the south-east, Chandpur formed a major production hub, with Lakshmipur and Noakhali also contributing substantially, highlighting the role of the Meghna estuarine network. The south-west region showed moderate but stable river fisheries, led by Bagerhat, followed by Khulna and Faridpur. In contrast, river fish production in the north-west remained limited, with only modest contributions from districts such as Sirajganj (Fig. 4). The eastern hill region exhibited consistently low to negligible river production over time, with Chattogram standing out as the sole district maintaining a noticeable level of river fisheries.

River fish production in Bhola, Barishal, and Chandpur has risen four, two, and three times over the last 19 years. In contrast, river fish production has been reduced in several districts of Bangladesh, especially in north-central and north-east regions, such as Dhaka, Gazipur, Mymensingh, Tangail, and Sylhet. River fish production in the north-central and north-eastern regions showed a consistent declining trend over time (Fig. 4). In Dhaka, river production increased during the early 2000s, peaked around 2010, and then declined in subsequent years. Gazipur exhibited a continuous reduction in river fish production across the study period.

Mymensingh, through which the Old Brahmaputra River flows, experienced a steady decrease in river fish output over the two decades. Tangail showed a sharp reduction within a short time span, with river production dropping markedly between the early and mid-2000s.
In the north-east, Sylhet also displayed a gradual decline in river fish production from 2001 to 2002 to 2019–2020 (Fig. 4a–e).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Comparative analysis between different production domains
ce:section.ce:para: Temporal analysis shows that pond production is continually growing; more importantly, the growth rate of pond production is higher than that of river production. Compared with pond production, the growth rate of river fish production was very slow. In 2005-2006, pond fish production reached 0.3 million MT, while river production was only 0.1 million MT, less than half of pond production (Fig. 5 a). Similarly, by 2010-2011, river fish production was still half of pond production (Fig. 5a).

In 2019-2020, river fish production saw a significant increase but did not surpass pond production (Fig. 5a). Throughout this period, pond aquaculture consistently outpaced river fish production every year. Pond fish production played a major role in total aquaculture production of Bangladesh, contributing 57%, compared to 28% from capture fisheries (Fig. 5b). Since capture fisheries production is dominated by river fish production, pond fish production makes a substantial contribution to the total national fish production, far surpassing that of river fish.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Forecasting of pond area, pond production, and river production in Bangladesh
ce:section.ce:para: According to ADF test, all three datasets were not stationary (>0.05) (Table S1). It implies the presence of a unit root, α = 1. In every instance, the p-values were less than 0.05 after the second difference, which is regarded as statistically significant (Table S1). From the ADF test, it can be concluded that the undifferenced and first differenced time series were not stationary, but the second differenced time series was stationary for all models (Fig. S2 and S3). Therefore, the d value of the time series data for the pond area, pond, and river production was 2.

The ACF and PACF of the pond area time-series data are shown in Fig. S2, indicating that the moving average order (q) cannot be more than three since the ACF drastically decreases after the second lag. Nevertheless, lag 3 has a slight intercept with the upper threshold line. PACF declined significantly after the first lag; therefore, the autoregressive order (p) cannot be more than 1 (Fig. S2). A set of candidates ARIMA models was first explored for each dataset - pond area, pond production, and river production - to identify suitable forecasting structures (Table 1 ). Model selection was guided by goodness-of-fit, with particular emphasis on the AIC [26]. Among the competing specifications, ARIMA (0, 2, 2) for pond area, ARIMA (1, 2, 0) for pond production, and ARIMA (2, 2, 1) for river production yielded the lowest AIC values and were therefore selected as the best-fitting models for their respective series.

These optimal models were subsequently used to generate forecasts for the period 2021–2030. Diagnostic checks confirmed the adequacy of the fitted models. Inspection of the residual autocorrelation functions (Fig. 6 ) and the results of the Ljung–Box tests indicated no significant autocorrelation in the residuals, with all p-values exceeding 0.05 for the selected models (Fig. 6a–c). Therefore, the residuals are not dependent, and the chosen models do not exhibit a lack of fit. In addition, Q-Q plot explained the normal distribution of residuals, which comprehensively supports the white noise of residuals (Fig. 6d, e, and 6f)

The application primarily employs time series in forecasting models to estimate future quantities and trends based on the trained dataset. This investigation aimed to establish the effective application of ARIMA model and attempted to predict the pond area, pond production, and river production. The forecast values were generated between 2021 and 2030. Tables S2, S3 and S4 show point forecasts and 95% prediction intervals obtained using the ARIMA models in Table 1. Lo95 and Hi95 are the lower and higher bounds of the prediction interval for the significance level α = 0.05. From these results (Table S2, S3 and S4), it indicates that the total pond area (Fig. 7 b), pond fish production (Fig. 7d), and river fish production (Fig. 7f) will show a continuous increase in the coming years. Based on the forecast, the pond area is expected to follow a rising trend in the next two decades. The ARIMA model forecast revealed that land acquired for pond construction will increase to 3.13% of Bangladesh's total area by 2030, which was 1.71% in 2001 (Fig. 7a and b). It is estimated that in 2030, the pond area will reach 4,65,113 ha (Fig. 7b–Table S2). By the year 2030, land acquisition for pond culture will have increased by approximately 75% from the year 2001. The forecast revealed that the pond and river production would be 2.77 (Fig. 7d–Table S3) and 0.6 million MT (Fig. 7f–Table S4), respectively. Both production trends are projected to increase annually. However, by 2030, river production will be four and a half (4.5) times less than pond production.

In the past two decades, pond area expanded by 52.35%, while pond aquaculture production soared by 199% increase, reflecting a fourfold increase in productivity. Factors driving this massive growth include conducive water and soil quality for fish production, the availability of quality fish seed and feed, and the availability of other essential aquaculture inputs [27].

In north-east and north-central regions, extensive fish farming was a traditional practice due to the availability of natural carp seed in the river Brahmaputra. Therefore, Mymensingh district, located in Bangladesh's north-central region, is at the forefront of pond expansions [28]. Over the last three decades, the rising rate of fish-ponds in the Mymensingh district by converting cropland has been significantly greater than that of national level. One key reason is that fish farming profits are often two to three times higher than rice cultivation [29,30]. Another study reported that fish farming in north-central region contributes the highest percentage of household income, compared to crop farming and other business [28,31]. The expansion of pond area in the north-central region (Mymensingh), driven by reduced wild fish availability, increased hatchery seeds, improved transport, market access, institutional efforts, research and development projects, such as the DANIDA-supported Mymensingh Aquaculture Extension Project [32,33], along with agglomeration effects, knowledge sharing, and the emerggcne of feed companies [27].

The pond area in the Dhaka district shrank, similar to the nearby Gazipur district. Dhaka, the capital city, is in a central region experiencing one of the highest population growth and urbanization trends among many other developing countries [34] and is home to over ten million people [35]. Consequently, these uncontrolled populations and industrialization have disrupted the pond-based aquaculture, resulting in declining production in Dhaka and Gazipur districts.

In the south-west, pond fish production is highest in Jashore, followed by Mymensingh in the north-central region. Although production costs were lower in Mymensingh, Jashore generated higher net returns and benefit-cost ratios, making pond aquaculture more lucrative there [36]. The expansion of land-use conversion from rice fields to shrimp farming became increasingly prominent over time [8,9,16].

In addition, with a substantial area suitable for prawn-finfish culture, expanding prawn farming in Chattogram has the potential to significantly boost the country's annual foreign exchange earnings. The majority of aquaculture inputs, such as feeds, chemicals, and antibiotics, are imported through the Chattogram seaport [37]. This ease of communication lowers input costs, followed by transportation costs, and encourages farmers in this region to engage in more pond farming in southeast region. The south-east's fertile, river-silt-enriched lands provide ideal conditions for pond aquaculture. In Cumilla, pond area doubled between 2001–02 and 2019–20, while low-lying terrain in Chandpur allows ponds to retain water year-round [38]. In Noakhali, the Meghna and Feni rivers are interconnected through canals, tributaries, streams, and creeks, and the coastline experiences a substantial tidal range. Together with favorable temperature, rainfall, and humidity, these environmental and climatic conditions have supported the extensive expansion of pond aquaculture in the region [39].

Aquaculture practices have not been popular in the Chattogram Hill Tracts region. According to our study, until 2009, no fish farming ponds were identified in the eastern hilly regions of Bangladesh. However, in 2010, 1106 ha, 452 ha, and 295 ha of pond areas were found in Khagrachari, Bandarban, and Rangamati, respectively (Fig. 2c). Some areas of ponds have existed in hilly regions, but the expansion is nearly halting. The transportation cost for feed and seeds purchased from remote areas was high in the hilly districts and perhaps such additional costs make culture fisheries less profitable, which may have diverted farmers from pond aquaculture [19].

This study reveals that over the past 19 years, south-central districts such as Barishal, Jhalokathi, Bhola, and Patuakhali have exhibited static conditions in terms of pond area expansion. Notably, the districts in the south-central area stood out in terms of riverine fish production (Fig. 5). Consumer studies indicate a preference for open-water fish over farmed fish in closed-water systems [40]. Therefore, if there is a significant supply of riverine fish in the market, the acceptance of pond culture fish will decrease, and riverine fish will become a strong competitor to farmed fish [41]. In contrast, capture fisheries, involving fishing in open water, tend to be more cost-effective than farmers fishes due to the absence of expenses related to construction, feed, seed, supplements, or management. This encourages fishermen and farmers to depend on wild catches for their livelihoods. Thus, it can be inferred that there is an inverse relationship between fish production from rivers and ponds in this region.

In the study period, the south-west part of Bangladesh experienced at least eight cyclonic storms. Climate change-induced natural disasters reduced pond fish and seed production in the south-western region, resulting in a low growth rate of culture fisheries during the years of cyclonic storms and the subsequent years [42].

Our study revealed that although river fish production is increasing, its growth rate is slowing, and its share of total fish production in Bangladesh remains relatively modest. Our spatiotemporal approach validated the disparities between pond and river fish production, consistent with findings from other studies [43,44]. Over the past two decades, human activities have significantly impacted river ecosystems, leading to habitat loss and degradation. As a result, many fish species have become critically endangered, river areas have shrunk, and the gap between pond and river fish production has widened [43,45], which also aligns with our findings in capture fisheries. Section 4.3 of this study provides policy recommendations to effectively address the issues for sustainable river production.

The seven north-west districts of Bangladesh are traversed by numerous transboundary rivers originating from India [46]. This study found that river fish production in this region did not exhibit a satisfactory increase; instead, it decreased over time. The decline in river areas and fish production in the north-west region is due to natural factors such as siltation, reduced depth, sand blockage, water retention, high water temperature, and the impact of climate change, which have harmed breeding grounds of fish [47]. Anthropogenic factors, including dredging, water pollution, pesticide use, and the discharge of industrial, agricultural, and municipal wastes, have degraded fish habitats along the north-western bank of the Padma River [48]. The Teesta and Farrakka Barrage have caused permanent damage to the Jamuna and Padma Rivers, destroying fish habitats, disrupting hilsa migrations, and negatively impacting river fish production [6,49].

The north-central region of Bangladesh comprises several districts through which many rivers and tributaries flow [47]. Most industries along these rivers discharge untreated waste directly into the river water, causing pollution, river encroachment, and reduced fish production in the adjacent rivers of the Dhaka district, and reducing the production of rivers [5,50]. The greater Sylhet region, comprising 16 districts, dominates the north-east part of Bangladesh. The spatiotemporal distribution of river production in this part of Bangladesh is minimal. The poor production of river fish is partly due to the construction of Tipaimukh Multipurpose Hydroelectric Dam in India. This dam causes some ecological problems by reducing water flow from Barak river, potentially leading to drying up the Surma and Kushiara rivers in Bangladesh [27]. Other consequences include reduced water depth, disrupted fish migration, deteriorated water quality, and a narrowed river channel, all contributing to decreased fish catch [51].

As per GIS mapping, the south-east and south-central districts of Bangladesh showed the highest river production compared to other districts. This is perhaps due to low industrialization, proximity to the Bay of Bengal, and particularly hilsa fishery conservation strategies taken by the DoF [52]. Due to the implementation of hilsa management projects, the abundance of large river catfish and other species has also increased remarkably [52]. Additionally, being at the mouth of the sea, these rivers have pollutants washed away into the Bay of Bengal by the current, resulting in relatively less polluted water, which is more suitable for the production of aquatic flora and fauna.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Future demand for aquaculture policy: different countries' perspectives
ce:section.ce:para: This study predicted the pond area, pond and river fish production up to 2030. Based on ARIMA (0, 2, 2), the forecasted data show that the pond area is expected to expand by 15% in 2030 from 2019. ARIMA (1, 2, 0) and ARIMA (2, 2, 1) show that pond and river production will also increase by 36.61% and 79.8% from 2020 to 2030. Land use for aquaculture ponds in Dongtan, Chongming Island, China, accounted for over 6%, 36%, and 39% in 1990, 1997, and 2000, respectively [53]. In Vietnam, 440 ha (approximately 60%) of mangrove areas were converted to shrimp farming between 1986 and 1992 [54]. In alignment with global trends, Damarpota in south-western Bangladesh, where 79% (274 ha) of the rice fields in the village were converted to shrimp ponds between 1985 and 2003 [16]. The construction of pond aquaculture necessitates conversion of land, including rice fields, other crop fields, mangrove forests, and various terrestrial ecosystems [8,9,16]. Reducing rice fields in Bangladesh to boost fish production would be counterproductive, given rice has importance as a staple food. Constructing aquaculture ponds without a strategic land use plan could pose significant future risks. Therefore, a national policy, similar to those in countries like Vietnam and Indonesia [55], is urgently needed in Bangladesh. The proposed policy should ensure sustainable land use practices by managing land under government supervision. To support aquaculture growth, China has introduced the ‘Outline of the National Marine Economic Development Plan’ and guidelines for accelerating green aquaculture. These initiatives focus on scientific advancement, careful planning, and conserving natural resources, like land, water and forests, rather than unlimited aquaculture expansion to address inefficiencies and extensive production [56]. Also, Canada enacted the Fisheries and Coastal Resources Act, 1996 to identify suitable areas of land-based aquaculture. The field-based aquaculture operator must submit a detailed Development Plan to obtain a license in Canada [57].

Bangladesh's first fishery act was established in 1950. Most of the regulations and laws were introduced in the last two decades after the adoption of the National Fisheries Policy (NFP) in 1998 [58]. In 1995, the leasing system for flowing rivers was abolished, making fishing free for all except those using mechanized boats. Although this policy aimed to benefit the poor fishers, the lack of control led to excessive fishing pressure, reducing river fish production. Section 5.8 of NFP, 1998 considers discharging harmful municipal and industrial waste directly into rivers and open waterbodies a punishable crime, but weak enforcement has undermined this policy. It also suggests careful planning and implementation of flood control and irrigation projects (section 6.1) to protect river ecosystems and fish breeding grounds. The policy encourages fish culture in haor, baor 3
3 A baor refers to a type of wetland or oxbow lake found in the floodplain areas of Bangladesh. and beel 4
4 A beel is also a type of wetland or natural depression found in the floodplain regions of Bangladesh. Beels are typically low-lying areas that accumulate water, either from rainfall, river overflow, or groundwater seepage, forming shallow lakes or marshes. after re-excavation (section 6.4, sections 6.10–6.13), and promotes integrated rice-fish cultivation to reduce pressure on pond culture (section 6.3 and 7.2). However, implementation of these laws and policies is hindered by unclear policy guidelines; inadequate legislation; poor enforcement; political interference, lack of community involvement, and infrastructural limitations [59,60].

To sustain production and growth while limiting new pond construction, the government, scientists, and policymakers must implement effective policies and regulations. Most rice fields in Bangladesh are being converted to ponds, leading to inefficient land use if exclusively dedicated to fish or rice. Early studies on the environmental impacts of aquaculture emphasized the need to minimize land use per unit of fish produced [61]. Therefore, promoting technologies that maximize fish production with minimal land use is essential. Integrating irrigated rice fields into the integrated aquaculture agriculture (IAA) can enhance land and water use efficiency, boosting productivity and sustainability. Pond-based IAA enhances farm productivity by 11% compared to traditional pond fish culture [62]. Additionally, aquaponics and vertical aqua-geoponics can support production growth without expanding land use, though they are energy-intensive and subject to uncertainty. Pen culture and cage cultures in open waterbodies offer higher environmental sustainability and productivity without requiring additional land [63].

The government of Bangladesh should launch initiatives to transfer aquaculture technologies to rural farmers to enhance pond productivity and reduce reliance on traditional fish farming. Furthermore, urgent action is needed to protect and restore rivers, ensuring their navigability and reducing pollution.

The primary limitation of this study is the small number of available training data points. The national fisheries database in Bangladesh provides only annual, country-level data for a relatively short time period. This limitation also highlights an important future need for more comprehensive and long-term fisheries, aquaculture, and fish ecology databases in Bangladesh. In-addition, as it relies on secondary, aggregated time-series data that may obscure local-level variability in pond area expansion and fish production across regions. The ARIMA models used for forecasting assume that historical trends and underlying relationships remain stable over time; therefore, the projections do not explicitly account for potential structural changes arising from climate variability, extreme events, policy interventions, technological innovations, market shocks, or transboundary water management decisions. In addition, ecological factors such as biodiversity loss, habitat degradation, and changes in fish migration patterns were not modeled quantitatively, and socio-economic drivers, including farmer behavior, input price fluctuations, and consumer preferences, were considered only indirectly. Consequently, while the forecasts provide useful insights into likely trends up to 2030, the results need to be complemented by future studies incorporating spatially disaggregated data, environmental indicators, and scenario-based modeling approaches.

To the best of our knowledge, this study marks the pioneering use of GIS mapping to analyze the past two decades of pond aquaculture and riverine fish production, combined with the application of the ARIMA model to forecast the forthcoming 10-year scenario of fish production and land use scenario. There has been no comprehensive research conducted on the comparative spatial relationship between pond production and river production, how these two systems, such as aquaculture and capture fisheries, are connected, and whether their relationship is proportional or inverse. In this study, we found that a huge amount of pond area is concentrated in north-central, south-west and south-east regions. However, in the north-central region, there has been a decline in pond area, pond production, and river production. The south-central part of Bangladesh showed a negative relationship between aquaculture and river fish production. High-capture fish production may lower the production of culture fisheries in the south-central part of Bangladesh. Land acquisition through pond construction accounted for 1.71% of Bangladesh's total area in 2001, increasing to 2.72% in 2019. By 2030, the ARIMA model forecasts that pond area in Bangladesh will cover 3.13% of the total land area throughout Bangladesh, reflecting an approximate 75% increase from 2001. Additionally, in 2030, the production of cultured fish is projected to reach 2.77 million MT, while capture fisheries production is expected to be 0.6 million MT. This study underscores the importance of implementing policies in the fish-producing regions to ensure the sustainable development of both aquaculture and capture fisheries production, preparing for future scenarios.
